newsitem.title: USA: State Sen says muni firms thumb noses at Rule G-37.
newsitem.headline: State Sen says muni firms thumb noses at Rule G-37.

text.p: New York State Senator Franz Leichter charged Monday that a new study shows that municipal securities firms continue to use soft money to "thumb their noses" at the MSRB's pay-to-play rule G-37.
Leichter, a Democrat from the Bronx, urged the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board to vote later this week to eliminate the soft-money "loophole" in the rule when it meets for a quarterly session.
Enacted in April 1994, rule G-37 generally bars muni dealers that contribute directly or indirectly to issuer clients from doing negotiated business with those municipalities for two years afterward.
Leichter aides studied New York State board of elections data for the first six months of 1997 and Federal Election Commmission data from 1995 through the present.

"There are easy ways to get around rule G-37, and securities firms are doing it left and right," Leichter aide Jonathan Bowles said. "If they want to make the rule truly effective, they need to toughen (it) up."

Among his findings, Leichter said that New York muni firms or their employees gave at least $3,000 to the Republican State Committee (RSC) in the first half of 1997, including a $2,000 donation from Samuel A. Ramirez & Co.
During the same period, the committee transferred $3.1 million to the campaign of Governor Pataki, Leichter said.

Leichter said the committee also raised at least $20,500 in "housekeeping," or soft money, contributions from six muni firms or employees during 1997, including a $10,000 donation from First American Municipals.
Leichter said that among committees that got big contributions from securities firms were the Republican National State Elections Committee and the National Republic Senatorial Committee.

The former, Leichter said, transferred at least $100,000 to Pataki's campaign and hundreds of thousands of dollars more to the New York State GOP. The latter, which Leichter said is controlled by D'Amato, transferred at least $1.9 million directly to Pataki's campaign, he said.
Leichter said another panel - Republican Governors Assn. Conference - got most of its contributions from muni firms.
